articles.intro: An air fryer earns its place when it makes a decent dinner easier. These are meal combinations to work from, rather than promises that a particular appliance will make you lose weight.
sections: Build a whole meal, not just the crispy bit

Start with something you want to eat, then add the parts that make it dinner. Chicken with potato wedges and peas; salmon with rice and broccoli; or chickpeas with peppers, a wrap and yoghurt dressing are three possible combinations. Use the oven, hob or microwave alongside the basket. There is no prize for fitting the entire meal into one machine.
Three dinners to try

Chicken and wedges: cut potatoes into similar pieces, add a little oil and seasoning, and cook according to the appliance instructions. Cook chicken separately if the basket cannot accommodate it safely. Add frozen peas or a bag of salad.

Fish and vegetables: cook a fish portion using its packet or a tested recipe, then serve with microwave rice and vegetables. Choose seasoning you like rather than buying a cupboard of ingredients for one meal.

Chickpea wraps: use drained canned chickpeas and sliced peppers with a spice mix you already have. Serve in a wrap with salad. This is a meal idea; timing depends on your appliance and the size of the ingredients.
The safety bit matters

Follow the appliance and food instructions. Leave room for hot air to circulate, keep raw meat away from ready-to-eat food and check that food is thoroughly cooked. A brown outside does not prove that the centre is safe. The Food Standards Agency explains how to check cooking and use a food thermometer. Do not use this page as a universal temperature or cooking-time chart.
Make the next evening easier

Keep one reliable combination on your shopping list. If a recipe needs ingredients you will never use again, simplify it. Frozen vegetables and plain microwave grains are useful options when time is short. Serve your portion onto a plate, sit down and decide whether it is enough before returning for more. You are making dinner easier to repeat, not turning it into a test of willpower.
sources: Food Standards Agency: cooking food safely

articles.intro: A barbecue can stay a barbecue. Put a few useful choices on the table, decide what you actually fancy and keep the food safe.
sections: Plan the table before lighting the grill

Alongside burgers or sausages, put out something that makes a complete plate: grilled vegetables, corn, a bean salad, potatoes or bread. There is no need to replace every favourite. A host can offer choices without announcing which guest ought to eat what.
A simple shopping plan
Choose the main food first. Buy for the people coming rather than for an imaginary eating competition.
Add two sides that you will enjoy eating: peppers and courgettes, a tomato salad, or canned beans with a dressing are options.
Keep sauces available separately so people choose their own amounts.
Put drinking water and alcohol-free options where they are easy to reach. Nobody needs to explain why they are having one.
Do not confuse charred with cooked

Keep raw meat separate from cooked food and use different utensils. Follow Food Standards Agency barbecue guidance: check the centre as well as the outside, and do not partly cook meat for finishing much later. Keep chilled food chilled until needed. Put salads and cooked food away from the plate that held raw meat.
Enjoy the meal and carry on

Pick the foods you came for and eat a plate you enjoy. If you have more than planned, the next meal can be an ordinary meal. There is no need for a punishment workout or a day without food. For next time, notice the practical problem: perhaps you arrived hungry, the only sides were crisps or drinks kept getting topped up. Change that detail rather than declaring the whole summer ruined.
sources: Food Standards Agency: barbecue food safety

articles.intro: Sometimes somebody else cooking is exactly what the evening needs. Make a takeaway choice that suits your appetite, budget and plans without writing off the week.
sections: Decide what you want before opening the app

Is it a particular dish, a night off cooking or food to share? Start there. Ordering while browsing every offer can turn one meal into several. Check the delivery fee and minimum spend as well as the menu price; adding food you do not want to qualify for an offer may cost more.
Useful changes by type of meal
Pizza: choose the pizza you want, then decide whether you actually need extra sides. Share a larger pizza if that fits the group; keep leftovers safely rather than feeling obliged to finish it.
Indian: compare grilled options, vegetable dishes and your favourite curry. Order rice and bread for the people eating rather than automatically adding both to every meal.
Chinese: consider a vegetable side and a main you enjoy. Ask for sauces separately if available. Dish names alone cannot tell you their calories or salt content.
Fish and chips or burgers: choose the size you want before the meal deal chooses it for you. Add a drink because you want one, rather than because it is the default.
Use information where it exists

Compare published nutrition information when a restaurant provides it, but do not invent a precise calorie count from a photograph. An allergy is a separate safety issue: contact the restaurant about ingredients and cross-contamination, even if you have ordered the dish before. A menu marked healthy does not establish that it is safe for your allergy.
Keep it an ordinary part of the week

A takeaway does not require compensation the next morning. If cost or frequency is becoming a problem, choose one practical change: keep an easy freezer dinner available, agree a takeaway night, or stop ordering extra food just to meet a discount. Keep the change specific enough that you can tell whether it helped.
sources: Food Standards Agency: food allergy and intolerance
next: Save an easy alternative in Grub

articles.intro: Meal prep is useful if it saves you time when you need it. You do not need identical tubs for seven days. Start by making two awkward meals easier.
sections: Choose the actual problem

Look at the next few days. Is lunch expensive, dinner late or breakfast missing altogether? Pick one of those. Preparing food for a different problem will leave you with a fridge full of good intentions. Decide how many portions you need and check your freezer space before shopping.
Prepare parts you can use twice
Cook a meal you already like in a larger batch, if the recipe can be safely scaled, and freeze the extra portions.
Prepare a dressing, a chopped vegetable or a sandwich filling rather than an entire week's menu.
Keep a backup requiring little preparation: soup and toast, eggs, or a bean-based meal are possible choices depending on your dietary needs.
Label portions with the food and date. Put tomorrow's lunch where you will remember to take it.
Storage is part of the plan

Follow the Food Standards Agency guidance on cooling, chilling and reheating. Cool cooked food promptly, refrigerate it within two hours and reheat leftovers only once until steaming hot throughout. Rice has specific storage precautions; use the linked guidance rather than applying a general rule to every ingredient. If you cannot use a portion within its safe storage time, freeze it promptly if suitable.
A realistic first attempt

On your next shop, buy for one dinner that also provides a second portion, plus an easy lunch. After eating them, ask what caused the most faff: chopping, containers, forgetting a portion or getting bored. Fix that one detail. If batch cooking makes your weekend miserable, there are other ways to keep weekday food simple.
sources: Food Standards Agency: chilling, freezing and defrosting
Food Standards Agency: safe storage and reheating
next: Build a shopping list in Grub

articles.intro: High cholesterol usually does not announce itself with a symptom. A blood test and a conversation about your overall risk are more useful than guessing from how you feel.
sections: Understand the result you have

Ask for the actual results and what they mean for you. Total cholesterol is only part of the picture; clinicians also consider the different cholesterol measurements and factors such as blood pressure, smoking, diabetes and family history. A result described as normal by one person is not a personalised treatment decision for somebody else.
Make a couple of food swaps

The NHS recommends reducing saturated fat and choosing foods such as wholegrains, vegetables, nuts and unsaturated oils. Put that into one ordinary meal: use an olive- or rapeseed-based spread instead of butter, or try beans or fish where you usually have fatty processed meat. Check labels on foods you buy often. You do not need to cut out all fat or buy supplements advertised as a substitute for treatment.
Take these questions to your appointment
What are my results, and what is my overall cardiovascular risk?
Does my family history suggest inherited high cholesterol?
What changes would make the most difference in my circumstances?
If medicine is recommended, what benefit and possible side effects should I understand?
When should my blood test or treatment be reviewed?
Do not make treatment conditional on weight loss

A clinician may recommend treatment even while you work on food, movement or smoking. Keep taking prescribed medicine unless your clinician advises otherwise. If you are worried about side effects, ask for a review instead of silently stopping. Save the result and the agreed next step somewhere you can find them; a number without a follow-up plan is easy to forget.
next: Read the men's Health MOT guide

articles.intro: Weight can affect blood pressure, but it is not the only factor and losing weight is not a reason to stop prescribed tablets yourself. Start with a reliable measurement and an agreed follow-up.
sections: Feeling fine does not tell you the reading

High blood pressure often has no symptoms. A pharmacy or GP check is useful even if you feel well. One reading may need confirmation through home or ambulatory monitoring. The NHS uses different thresholds for clinic and home readings; use the interpretation given by your healthcare professional rather than choosing whichever number looks better.
If you are measuring at home

Use a validated upper-arm monitor with the right cuff size and follow the instructions you have been given. Sit quietly, support your arm and avoid talking during the measurement. Keep a record of the readings, dates and circumstances, including any symptoms. Bring the record and your medicine list to your review. A rushed measurement after climbing the stairs is not the same as a properly taken resting reading.
Choose a change you can repeat
Compare salt on foods you buy regularly and try a lower-salt alternative you enjoy.
Fit a manageable walk or another suitable activity into the week.
If you smoke, ask about stop-smoking support.
Discuss alcohol and any medicine or supplement that may affect blood pressure with your clinician.
Ask when to review both readings and treatment if your weight changes.
Know when a reading is not the main issue

Sudden chest pain that does not go away, particularly with breathlessness, sweating or pain spreading to an arm or jaw, needs emergency help: call 999. Do not wait to repeat a blood-pressure reading or leave a message in My Timber. For other worrying symptoms or very high readings, seek prompt medical advice following the instructions from your clinician and the linked NHS guidance.
sources: NHS: high blood pressure and urgent symptoms

articles.intro: Being told you are at increased risk of type 2 diabetes is a reason to make a plan, not a verdict about your character. Find out which test was done, what the result means and what support is available.
sections: Ask for the result and its meaning

Prediabetes is commonly used for blood glucose above the usual range but below the threshold for diabetes. Your clinician should interpret the result, including whether a repeat or different test is needed. Do not diagnose yourself from a borrowed glucose meter, and do not assume a risk result means you already have type 2 diabetes.
Turn the conversation into a plan
Ask which test you had, your result and when it should be checked again.
Discuss family history, medicines and other health conditions that may affect risk or advice.
Ask what diabetes-prevention support you are eligible for locally. NHS arrangements differ across the UK.
Choose one food change and one manageable way to move more, rather than starting an extreme diet.
If tracking numbers makes you anxious or compulsive, tell the clinician and agree a simpler approach.
Make the first change ordinary

You might start with a breakfast you can manage on a workday, vegetables alongside a familiar dinner, or a short walk at a time that usually works. The useful question is what you can repeat. If cost, disability, shift work or caring responsibilities make the advice difficult, name the obstacle and ask for a plan that takes it into account.
Risk reduction is not a guarantee

Lifestyle support can reduce the chance of developing type 2 diabetes, but nobody can promise that a particular person will avoid it. Keep the agreed checks. If you develop symptoms such as unusual thirst, passing urine more often or unexplained weight loss, seek medical advice rather than waiting for your next routine review. If you already have diabetes or take glucose-lowering medicine, changes to treatment belong with your clinician.

articles.intro: BMI is your weight in kilograms divided by your height in metres squared. It can help identify health risk, but it cannot tell you your fitness, your worth or the whole story of your health.
sections: Use the right calculation

Enter a recent weight and measured height into an adult calculator, checking the units. BMI does not directly measure body fat or where it is carried. Pregnancy, age, muscle mass and some medical circumstances affect interpretation. A very muscular person and somebody with little muscle can have the same BMI for different reasons.
Thresholds need context

For many adults, BMI 25 to 29.9 is classified as overweight and 30 or above as obesity. Risk can occur at lower BMI in some ethnic groups, so an adult calculator may ask about ethnicity. These are assessment categories, not a verdict about one person or automatic eligibility for a particular medicine.
Look beyond the single number
Ask about waist measurement and waist-to-height ratio where appropriate; these add information about central fat.
Consider blood pressure, cholesterol, blood glucose, family history and symptoms with a clinician.
Notice practical progress too: what you can do, how you feel and whether a plan is sustainable.
If you are older, frail or losing weight unintentionally, ask for individual assessment rather than trying to reach a calculator category.
Make it useful without making it your identity

Write down the question behind the calculation. Perhaps you want to understand a GP result, compare treatment options or decide whether to book a health check. Take that question to the appropriate professional. Recalculating BMI every day is unlikely to answer it. If weighing or measuring is causing distress, you can seek support without supplying a perfect set of numbers first.
sources: NHS: adult BMI calculator and limitations

articles.intro: Looking after your heart starts with a few checks and changes you can keep doing. You do not need to become an athlete before asking about your blood pressure, cholesterol or family history.
sections: Check what you cannot feel

High blood pressure and high cholesterol can be present without obvious symptoms. Ask your GP or a suitable pharmacy about checks and bring a list of your medicines. Tell the clinician about close relatives who developed heart disease at a young age. A wearable's reassuring reading does not rule out heart disease.
Choose the change with the most useful support

If you smoke, ask about a stop-smoking service. If moving more is the next step, choose something suitable for your current ability and build gradually. Compare foods you eat regularly for saturated fat and salt rather than buying products labelled heart healthy. If a clinician recommends medicine, discuss its benefits and risks; food and exercise changes do not automatically replace it.
Questions worth taking with you
Which checks do I need, and how do the results fit together?
Does my family history change the plan?
What activity is appropriate given my symptoms or conditions?
What is the next review date, and who do I contact about side effects?
If a suggested change is difficult because of money, pain or caring responsibilities, what is a realistic alternative?
Act on symptoms, not just numbers

Call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not go away, especially with sweating, breathlessness, nausea or pain spreading to an arm, jaw or back. Do not drive yourself or wait for SHIFT to reply. New or worsening symptoms need appropriate medical assessment even if your last blood test was reassuring. This page supports a conversation about prevention; it does not diagnose chest pain.

articles.intro: Start from the amount of walking you can comfortably manage now. The plan below is a flexible example, not a prescription or a challenge you have to complete on schedule.
sections: Pick a route you can actually use

Choose somewhere familiar with a manageable surface, places to stop and a way home. Think about weather, lighting, toilets and whether you want company. A short loop near home can be more useful than an impressive route that leaves you stranded when tired.
A first fortnight, with permission to repeat
First few outings: try a short, comfortable walk. Five minutes is an option if that suits your ability; less is fine too. Notice how you feel during the walk and afterwards.
For the rest of the first week: repeat the amount that felt manageable at a time that fits. Rest or use another suitable activity if needed.
In the second week: if you are recovering comfortably, add a little time to one outing. Keep the others familiar. If it feels too much, repeat or reduce the earlier amount.
After that: build gradually in a way you can sustain. Missing a day does not create a debt to repay with a much longer walk.
Effort matters more than a step-count contest

The NHS adult activity guidance gives a longer-term target of 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly, alongside strength activity. It is a direction to build towards, not a minimum entry requirement. At moderate intensity you can usually talk but not sing. Walking pace and suitable duration depend on you; a phone's step target does not know your health or recovery.
Know when to ask first

If you have been inactive for some time, have a medical condition or are unsure what is suitable, speak to a healthcare professional. Stop and get appropriate help for concerning symptoms. Sudden chest pain or severe breathlessness is not something to push through. If walking is inaccessible, ask about seated activity, swimming or another option that suits you.

articles.intro: Home strength work can start with simple movements and a safe space. The first job is finding an exercise you can do comfortably, not proving how much you used to lift.
sections: Set up before the first repetition

Use a clear, non-slip space and stable equipment. A chair should be solid, not wheeled, and positioned so it cannot slide. Do not improvise resistance-band anchors on handles or furniture that might fail. Read the equipment instructions and check for damage.
Start with a few suitable movements

A sit-to-stand from a stable chair or a wall press-up may be an option, depending on your ability. Use a reputable exercise guide to learn the movement and select an easier version if needed. Try a small comfortable amount, with control, rather than rushing to fatigue. There is no universal number of repetitions appropriate for every reader.
Make progress understandable
Record the movement and version you tried so you can repeat it.
Rest enough to keep the next attempt controlled.
Change one thing at a time: perhaps a few more comfortable repetitions, a slightly different version or a little resistance.
Keep ordinary breathing and stop if pain or concerning symptoms develop.
If pain, balance, disability or an existing condition makes the choice uncertain, ask a qualified professional for individual advice.
Keep it small enough to return to

The NHS recommends strength activity on at least two days a week for adults, alongside aerobic activity. You can build towards that. Pick a place in your week when the setup is easy and leave yourself a note of what worked. My Timber can help organise your choices, but a published exercise card is not personal trainer or medical clearance.

articles.intro: You can enjoy football without treating the first game back as a trial for your old team. Start with the version you can return to next week.
sections: Choose the right game

Ask about the session before turning up: its pace, contact rules, breaks, pitch surface and what happens if you need to stop. Walking football or a casual skills session may fit better than a full match. The label over-40s does not tell you how demanding the game will be.
Build towards playing

Before a match, try suitable walking or other manageable activity and see how you recover. Add simple strength work appropriate to your ability. For a first session, agree a shorter stint or a substitute role rather than relying on pride to decide when to stop. Warm up gradually using the session organiser's appropriate routine; old injuries and current pain deserve consideration.
Make the arrangements practical
Choose footwear suitable for the surface and check the pitch conditions.
Tell the organiser about limits they need to know, without sharing more personal information than necessary.
Bring water and make travel home straightforward.
Leave recovery time before another hard session.
Judge the session by whether it was enjoyable and manageable, rather than by the quickest bloke on the pitch.
Do not use the game to test worrying symptoms

If you have been inactive, have a medical condition or are uncertain what exertion is appropriate, get individual advice first. Football can be vigorous activity. Stop for concerning symptoms; sudden chest pain, collapse or severe breathing difficulty needs emergency help. A game is not the place to find out whether an unexplained symptom is harmless.

articles.intro: Weight-management medicines attract confident claims from people who have never seen your medical history. Separate the question of suitability from the noise around it.
sections: Myth: the brand names are interchangeable

Different medicines, formulations and licensed uses are not interchangeable. A medicine prescribed for diabetes is not automatically the same treatment plan as a medicine prescribed for weight management. Use the exact name and formulation on your prescription and ask your prescriber about any proposed change. Do not convert doses from a social-media chart.
Myth: a stronger dose is always a better dose

Dose progression and treatment decisions need individual assessment. Side effects are not proof that a treatment is working, and being able to tolerate one dose does not authorise the next. Follow your prescription and the patient leaflet. Ask your prescriber about missed doses, interruptions or troublesome symptoms rather than improvising.
Myth: medicines make everyday support irrelevant

Licensed weight-management treatment is used with changes to food and activity, not as a guarantee of a particular result. Practical support can still help with shopping, routine, movement and remembering your questions. That everyday support does not replace monitoring or turn a coach into a prescriber.
Myth: everybody regains the same amount after stopping

Research describes groups studied under particular conditions. It cannot predict your result from a short online story. If you are considering stopping because of cost, side effects or a change in provider, arrange a plan with the prescriber. Keep a record of the medicine, dose and last use so a new clinician can assess the situation.
Check the claim before buying

Ask who is prescribing, which registered pharmacy is dispensing, what the full cost is and how you obtain clinical advice. Avoid products sold as research peptides or compounded copies presented as equivalent to a UK-authorised medicine. SHIFT's information and My Timber are not a route to bypass assessment or prescribe treatment.
sources: Research: STEP 1 extension after semaglutide withdrawal
next: Read what to do if your clinic stops replying

articles.intro: Looking a certain way is a personal preference. It is not a complete health check and it is not the price of joining in with your own life.
sections: Name the thing you actually want back

Try a concrete answer: walking with your partner, carrying shopping more comfortably, joining a game or having enough energy for an evening out. You can still have an appearance goal, but giving it company makes the plan less dependent on a mirror.
Keep health checks separate from photographs

A photograph cannot establish your blood pressure, cholesterol, fitness or mental wellbeing. If you have symptoms or concerns, seek an appropriate health check. A lean appearance does not rule out a health problem, and a larger body does not tell somebody else what activity you can do.
Choose progress you can notice
Pick an activity you want to make easier and write down what is difficult about it now.
Choose a manageable food or movement change that connects to that goal.
Review how the change feels as well as whether you repeated it.
Include rest, enjoyment and relationships in the picture.
If comparison posts leave you feeling worse, change what you follow or take a break from the feed.
Do not wait to deserve support

You can ask about your health, buy comfortable clothes or take part in a suitable activity at your current size. If worries about shape, eating or exercise are becoming consuming, speak to a healthcare professional. More tracking is not always the useful answer. My Timber can organise an ordinary next step; it does not diagnose body-image or eating problems.
sources: NHS: overweight and obesity, including support
next: Choose your next step in My Timber

articles.intro: The joke about a dad bod can miss what is going on underneath: time pressure, changing routines, discomfort or worry. You can take those things seriously without treating your body as a punchline.
sections: Separate the joke from the problem

What is bothering you? Clothes, breathlessness, pain, tiredness, a health result or comments from other people may need different responses. Write down the issue in plain language. New or persistent symptoms deserve medical advice rather than being explained away as getting older.
Look at the week you have

Parenting can make uninterrupted time scarce. Identify one pinch point: finishing children's leftovers, skipping lunch then arriving home starving, or losing the only time you had to move. You do not need to fix all of family life before changing one routine.
Make a change that fits around the household
Plan an easy meal that everyone can adapt rather than cooking a separate diet dinner.
Agree a short period of time for your own activity with the people sharing the workload.
Keep a useful snack or lunch available for the day that overruns.
Choose an activity you can do with somebody if company makes it easier.
Ask for help with a practical task, not permission to care about your health.
Keep your children out of the judgement

Talk about energy, enjoyment and looking after yourself rather than describing bodies as good or bad. You can set a personal goal without making the family's food a moral test. If the plan is exhausting everyone, simplify it. Being a parent does not remove your need for support, and an ordinary setback does not cancel the example you are trying to set.
sources: NHS: healthy eating for everyday life
next: Find one step for this week

articles.intro: Weight and confidence can become tangled together. A change on the scales may matter to you, but you do not have to put the rest of your life on hold until it happens.
sections: Find the situation you are avoiding

Is it being photographed, buying clothes, going swimming or seeing friends? Pick one real situation rather than trying to become a completely confident person. Ask what would make it more manageable: different clothing, company, a quieter time or permission to leave early.
Make the first attempt smaller

If a full event feels too much, arrange a brief visit or choose a familiar place. If buying clothes is the issue, start with one comfortable item in the size that fits now. These are possible practical steps, not treatment for an anxiety or eating disorder. You decide which, if any, feel useful.
Keep two kinds of progress
Record changes towards your chosen health goal if tracking is helpful.
Also notice participation: a visit made, an invitation accepted or a question asked.
Avoid making every good day dependent on weighing less.
Tell a trusted person which comments are unhelpful and what support you would prefer.
If a setback happens, review the situation rather than deciding it proves something about you.
Ask for more support when needed

Persistent low mood, anxiety, body-image distress or difficulties around eating deserve support in their own right. A healthcare professional can help you choose an appropriate route. You do not need to wait for weight loss first. My Timber is a place to organise everyday goals and feedback; it is not a mental-health assessment or a substitute for care.

articles.intro: You do not need a polished explanation before asking for help. Start with the person or service most likely to help with the problem you actually have.
sections: Choose the kind of help

A mate may be the right person for company or a lift. A manager may help with a work arrangement. Health symptoms, medicine questions or persistent mental-health difficulties need an appropriate healthcare professional. One person does not have to supply every kind of support.
Use a sentence you could actually say
To somebody you trust: ‘I've been finding things difficult. Could we have a chat this week?’
For a practical favour: ‘Could you come with me to the appointment? I keep putting it off.’
To a GP: ‘This has been happening for a while and it is affecting my day. I'd like help working out what to do.’
If speaking feels difficult, write the main points before the appointment and take them with you.
Make the request specific

Say what would help next: listening for ten minutes, making an appointment, looking after the children while you attend, or checking in on Friday. You can say that you do not want advice yet. You can also ask about confidentiality and what a service records before sharing sensitive details.
If the first answer disappoints you

A poor response from one person does not settle whether you deserve support. Try another suitable person or service and explain what happened. For ongoing health concerns, ask how to obtain a review. SHIFT can help organise an everyday next step, but a check-in is not monitored clinical care and a company inbox is not an urgent route. Use the appropriate urgent or emergency service if immediate safety is at risk.
sources: NHS: preparing for a GP appointment
next: Find support routes in Good to Talk

articles.intro: Looking after other people can fill every spare corner of the week. Your own needs still count, even when there is no neat gap waiting for them.
sections: Identify the part you keep postponing

It might be a health appointment, eating lunch, some sleep or seeing somebody you enjoy. Choose one. A plan to start looking after yourself in general is hard to act on; booking one appointment or arranging one break is more concrete.
Make the workload visible

Write down the commitments that regularly consume the time you expected to have. Discuss one change with the people involved. Could a task be shared, a meeting moved or a regular break protected? If you are a carer, ask your local services about support available to you rather than assuming you must manage alone.
Ask for a practical arrangement
‘I need to attend this appointment. Can we work out cover for that hour?’
‘I'm finding the evenings difficult. Can we split this task differently?’
‘I'd like a short break on Saturday. Which time can we make work?’
If the answer is no, ask what alternative is possible instead of abandoning the need altogether.
Do not turn self-care into another performance

You do not need a perfect morning routine on top of an already overloaded day. A sandwich, a brief rest or making the call you have avoided may be enough for the first step. If exhaustion, mood or symptoms persist, seek appropriate advice. A small routine cannot resolve an unsafe workload or replace healthcare; getting support can be part of the plan.
sources: NHS: looking after yourself as a carer

articles.intro: Motivation can get you started. A useful routine gives you something to do on the day you do not feel particularly motivated. Keep it flexible enough to survive ordinary life.
sections: Connect the action to an event

Choose a cue that already happens: after lunch, when you put the kettle on or when you get home. Attach one small action to it. For example, prepare tomorrow's lunch after dinner or put walking shoes by the door before bed. Pick something that fits your circumstances; these are examples, not rules.
Give the routine a smaller version

Decide in advance what counts on a difficult day. A shorter suitable walk, a simpler dinner or recording a brief check-in may keep the thread. The smaller version should still serve the goal. It is not a way to force activity through illness, injury or exhaustion.
Review the arrangement, not your character
If you forgot, change the reminder or put the equipment somewhere useful.
If it took too long, shorten the action or choose a different time.
If you disliked it, try a genuinely different option rather than the same plan with a new slogan.
If other people keep interrupting the time, discuss the arrangement with them.
If it helped, keep it long enough to learn whether it fits most weeks.
Restart without a punishment lap

Missing a day gives you information about the plan. It does not require twice the exercise or less food tomorrow. Return at the next suitable opportunity and adjust what got in the way. My Timber lets you record a next step and whether it helped; keep the feedback honest so the next choice is based on your week rather than an imagined perfect one.

articles.intro: Feeling like yourself again can mean being able to join in, enjoy an evening or trust the next step. SHIFT's job is to help make that step usable in the life you have.
sections: Start with the ordinary thing you miss

It could be a walk with somebody, clothes that feel comfortable, cooking without a long debate or enough energy for a hobby. Give the goal a real setting. ‘Have more confidence’ becomes easier to work with when you know where you want to use it.
Use the part of SHIFT that fits
My Timber: keep a goal, choose a Next Shift and return to say whether it helped.
Grub: explore food choices and meal planning for the time and ingredients you have.
Fit: look for movement options suited to your circumstances; get individual advice when suitability is uncertain.
The Knowledge Hub: understand a topic and prepare questions for the right professional.
Good to Talk: read about difficult weeks and find appropriate support routes.
Keep responsibility clear

Everyday planning belongs with you. Diagnosis, prescribing, medicine changes and clinical monitoring belong with the appropriate healthcare professional. A saved check-in does not mean somebody is watching over it. If you have an urgent problem, use the appropriate urgent or emergency service rather than waiting for a reply from SHIFT.
Make the next step yours

Choose one thing that would make the next few days better, then decide how small it needs to be to fit. You can use My Timber, a notebook or your own notes. You do not need to buy medicine or an optional product to use the core My Timber check-in. For the experience behind the brand, read Matt's own story; his result is a personal account rather than a prediction for anybody else.

articles.intro: SHIFT began with Matt's experience of weight, pain, grief and getting help. The purpose is practical: somewhere to keep the thread when the first burst of enthusiasm has passed.
sections: The story behind the idea

In his approved personal account, Matt describes losing around four and a half stone over about eleven months through changes to food, movement and prescribed treatment following a clinical assessment. He also describes what the weight alone cannot explain: pain, drinking, grief and difficulty with everyday things. Read the full story in his own words on the About page. It is not a claim that another person will have the same result.
The middle needs support too

Starting gets plenty of attention. Keeping going when work changes, money is tight or a plan stops fitting can be harder to organise. SHIFT is intended to help you keep your reason for starting, remember what you tried and choose the next useful action without rebuilding the whole plan each time.
What that means in the product
My Timber keeps an everyday goal, a Next Shift and feedback about whether it helped.
Grub and Fit make food and movement choices easier to organise.
Life Back keeps the ordinary things you want to do in view.
The Knowledge Hub should help you understand questions and find the underlying sources, with clinical responsibilities made clear.
Free core tools remain useful whether or not you buy an optional product or use a treatment route.
